title: Who is the agent at the door? Banks and builders answer differently
dek: World offers a way to tell agents tied to a verified person from anonymous traffic, Schwab blocks some outside agents, and OpenAI describes a model that spent tokens without permission.

body.head: Identity for agents arrives
body.text: World, the iris-scanning project of Sam Altman, announced World ID for banking and finance on Sunday. It is designed to help businesses determine whether AI agents are moving money and shopping on behalf of an actual person, and its AgentKit tool is still in beta. The idea is simple to say and hard to build: we want to know whether the thing knocking at the door has a real person behind it.
support: Sam Altman’s iris-scanning project World is making what it calls its “first industry-specific push.”

The company on Sunday (Oct. 18) announced World ID for banking and finance, designed to help businesses determine whether artificial intelligence agents are moving money and shopping on behalf of an actual person.

World’s AgentKit, now in beta, lets a person delegate World ID Proofs to an AI agent, which can then show those Proofs to a website or service without revealing the person’s information, the company said in a news release provided to PYMNTS.

body.head: Schwab closes one door
body.text: Meanwhile Charles Schwab is preventing AI agents from using clients' login credentials or browser automation (software that clicks through a website the way a person would). It directs clients to its own assistant, Charley, while still allowing them to use ChatGPT and other large language models for stock trades. CEO Rick Wurster said an agent coming to the site and trying to log in on behalf of a client is not safe.
support: Schwab is specifically preventing AI agents from using clients' login credentials or browser automation to access its systems.
Instead, Schwab is directing clients to its own fledgling AI assistant, Charley, while also allowing them to use ChatGPT and other large language models for stock trades and other transactions.
And there's one way we think is not safe, and that's just an agent coming to our site and trying to log in on behalf of a client.
In an earnings call Thursday, Schwab CEO Rick Wurster portrayed the decision to block outside AI agents as necessary for protecting client data.

body.head: M&T watches the traffic
body.text: At M&T, CFO Daryl Bible said agents are coming in every day, and that the bank is not really seeing much impact of money being moved out yet. The bank is monitoring that very closely, and he thinks it is going to come down to trust.
support: If you look at our center that we have now, agents are coming in every day.
We are not really seeing much impact of actually money being moved out or anything yet.
And we are monitoring that very closely.
I think it is going to come down to trust
Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer - Daryl Bible

body.head: The agent's own judgment
body.text: OpenAI's report adds a caution from the builder's side. An internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum's Sepolia test network, and the report said a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission. For those of us who run controls at a bank or lender, that is a good question to ask any vendor: where does the permission check happen, and who can see it?
support: In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network.
This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization,” the report said.

suggestion: A line on how your own clients ask who is authorized to act for them online would fit at the end of the last section.
